title: Iran War Drives Gas to $4.50, Inflation Hits 3-Year High
summary: The 10-week-old war with Iran is hitting American wallets hard. On Tuesday, the Labor Department reported that consumer prices rose 3.8% in April from a year earlier—the biggest jump in three years. The main culprit? Gasoline. Prices at the pump averaged over $4.50 a gallon, a staggering 44% increase from last year. The spike stems from Iran's closure of the Strait of Hormuz, through which a fifth of the world's oil and liquefied natural gas flows. When the U.S. and Israel attacked Iran on February 28, Tehran retaliated by blocking this vital chokepoint, sending energy prices soaring. Month-over-month, overall prices rose 0.6% from March, with gasoline alone up 5.4%. While core inflation—excluding volatile food and energy—rose a milder 0.4% monthly and 2.8% annually, the pain at the pump is undeniable. For many Americans, it's a financial squeeze. Heather Long, chief economist at Navy Federal Credit Union, noted that inflation is now erasing all wage gains for the first time in three years. "There is a real financial squeeze underway," she wrote. "Middle-class and lower-income households are having to cut back on spending and stretch every dollar." The war has also rattled the Federal Reserve, which had been expected to cut interest rates this year. Now, the Fed is cautious, waiting to see if energy costs spill into broader prices. President Trump has criticized the Fed for not cutting rates, but his nominee for chair, Kevin Warsh, faces a tough balancing act. Some companies are already hurting: Whirlpool reported a nearly 10% revenue drop, blaming a "recession-level industry decline" from the war. For everyday people, it means tough choices. One woman described cutting back on "frill spending" and feeling the pinch even on her short commute. With midterm elections looming in November, inflation is set to be a key issue, testing whether voters blame the administration for the economic strain.
why_it_matters: The Iran conflict shows how distant geopolitical moves directly shape the price of gas, erode family budgets, and even decide elections—revealing the tight links between foreign policy and everyday life that affect a student’s future job market and cost of living.

background_read: The Strait of Hormuz (a narrow waterway between Oman and Iran) is one of the world’s most critical oil chokepoints; historically, threats to close it—such as during the Iran-Iraq War in the 1980s—have spiked global oil prices.

The Federal Reserve (the U.S. central bank that manages interest rates) was widely expected to cut rates in 2025, but a war-driven energy shock makes policymakers cautious because cutting rates too early could worsen inflation.
Kevin Warsh, Trump’s nominee for Fed chair, is a former Fed governor and Wall Street advisor who would face the difficult task of balancing low unemployment against rising prices.

Inflation eroding wage gains—as noted by economist Heather Long—means that even if workers get raises, the actual purchasing power of their paychecks falls, a phenomenon last seen during the post-pandemic recovery in 2022.

Midterm elections often hinge on pocketbook issues: when gas prices surge, voters historically tend to punish the party controlling the White House, making the November election a test of public patience with the war’s economic fallout.
Article_Structure: LEAD: Consumer prices jumped 3.8% in April, the biggest inflation spike in three years, driven by $4.50+ gasoline.
CAUSE: Iran closed the Strait of Hormuz after the U.S.-Israel attack on February 28.
├─ DETAIL: Strait carries a fifth of the world’s oil and liquefied natural gas; Tehran’s retaliation blocked it.
└─ IMPACT: Gasoline alone rose 5.4% monthly, pushing overall prices up 0.6% from March.
ECONOMIC INDICATORS: Core inflation milder (2.8% annually), but pain at the pump undeniable.
├─ WAGE EFFECT: Heather Long says inflation now erases all wage gains for the first time in three years.
└─ HOUSEHOLD: Middle-class and lower-income families cut back on frill spending.
POLICY DILEMMA: Federal Reserve hesitant to cut interest rates amid rising energy costs.
├─ TRUMP’S PUSH: President criticizes Fed for not cutting; nominee Kevin Warsh faces a balancing act.
└─ COMPANY DISTRESS: Whirlpool reports nearly 10% revenue drop, calling it a recession-level decline.
POLITICAL DIMENSION: Looming midterm elections frame inflation as a key issue.
└─ VOTER SENTIMENT: Testing whether the administration is blamed for the economic strain.

perspectives.description: Some argue that the crisis could accelerate a shift toward domestic renewable energy and electric vehicles, reducing long-term dependence on unstable oil chokepoints. Higher gas prices might also push consumers to choose more fuel-efficient cars.

For working families, a 44% rise in gas prices means less money for food, rent, and education. Hedge-fund managers and energy companies might profit, but lower- and middle-class Americans bear the brunt, as confirmed by Heather Long’s wage-erasure analysis.

Historically, oil supply shocks—like the 1973 OPEC embargo—triggered recessions, but modern economies are more diverse. The Fed’s wait-and-see approach reflects the tricky dance of not stifling growth while preventing an inflationary spiral, a pattern seen in past oil crises.

With midterm elections approaching, if inflation remains high, voters may shift Congressional control, changing the direction of economic policy. The conflict might also spur diplomatic pressure on Iran, or the Fed might be forced to cut rates after all if the economy weakens further.
